pages.title: Home
pages.content:
A community for people who make things

Make something. Share it by the fire.

Campfire is a friendly forum for woodworkers, welders, potters, tinkerers and everyone with sawdust in their pockets. Ask the beginner question, post the wobbly first project, swap tips with people who have been there.

Browse the forums
Join the circle

How the circle works

Three things we care about

Show your work

Finished pieces, works in progress and glorious failures are all welcome. Photos and sketches help everyone learn.

Ask anything

There are no silly questions about glue, grit or grounding. Somebody here asked the same thing last year.

Pass it on

When a reply solves your problem, say so. When you learn a trick, write it down for the next person.

pages.title: Community Guidelines
pages.content:
Campfire works because people are generous with what they know. These few rules keep it that way.

Be kind, especially to beginners

  • Assume good intent. Everyone was new once.
  • Critique the work, never the person. Say what works before what could be better.
  • No gatekeeping about tools or budgets. A hand saw and patience is a valid workshop.

Make your posts easy to help with

  • Use a clear title: “Glaze crawling on the rim” beats “Help!!”.
  • Say what you tried, what you expected and what happened instead.
  • Post in the forum that fits best. Moderators may move topics.

Safety first

  • Never advise someone to remove a guard or skip protective gear.
  • Mains electricity, gas and pressure vessels: point people to a qualified professional when in doubt.

No spam, no selling without asking

Sharing your own project page is fine. Advertising, affiliate links and unsolicited offers are removed. Ask a moderator before posting anything for sale.

Questions about these rules? Post in the forums or reply to the welcome topic.

pages.title: About Campfire
pages.content:
Campfire started as a group chat between four friends who shared a rented workshop on Fridays. When the chat got too busy to scroll, we moved it here.

Today the circle is a few hundred makers across a dozen countries. Some sell their work; most of us just like making things with our hands and talking about it afterwards.

Who keeps the fire going

The forum is run by volunteers. Ozan moderates the workshop forums and answers more welding questions than anyone should. If something needs attention, use the report link on any post or write to the moderators in the Lounge.

Built with Pursae

The site runs on Pursae with Pursae Forum: no tracking scripts, no ads, and pages that load fast on a phone in a garage with one bar of signal.

topics.author: admin
topics.title: Welcome to Campfire: start here
topics.content:
Welcome to the circle! A few things to help you settle in:

  • Introduce yourself in Introductions. Tell us what you make and what you want to learn.
  • Read the community guidelines. They are short, we promise.
  • When a reply helps you, say thanks and post a photo of the result. That is how the fire keeps burning.

Pull up a seat.

replies.author: mara
replies.content: Thanks for setting this up. Much easier to find things than in the old group chat.

replies.author: tomas
replies.content: Finally a place where nobody laughs at my welds. Well, not out loud.

topics.author: mara
topics.title: Hello from a one-car garage in Gothenburg
topics.content:
Hi all! I'm Mara. I carve spoons and bowls in the evenings and I'm slowly working up the courage to build a proper workbench. Most of my tools are hand tools: two chisels, a rasp, a Japanese pull saw and a hatchet I inherited from my grandfather.

Looking forward to learning from you.

replies.author: ozan
replies.content: Welcome, Mara! A grandfather's hatchet is the best possible starting tool. Post your spoons when you can.

replies.author: priya
replies.content: Spoon carving is so satisfying. Do you use green wood? I have been wanting to try birch.

replies.author: mara
replies.content: Yes, mostly green birch and cherry from a friend's garden. Birch is lovely to carve, just keep the blanks in a plastic bag so they don't crack.

topics.author: mara
topics.title: Hand-cut dovetails: my first ten attempts
topics.content:
I cut ten practice dovetail joints in pine this week. The first three had gaps you could post a letter through. By number eight they were almost tight.

What helped most:

  1. Marking with a knife instead of a pencil.
  2. Sawing on the waste side of the line, every time.
  3. Paring the baseline in two passes instead of one big chop.

What I still struggle with is keeping the saw square to the face. Any tips?

replies.author: ozan
replies.content: Great progress. For squareness, put a small mirror behind the board: you see the saw and its reflection, and it's obvious when they don't line up.

replies.author: tomas
replies.content: Also check that the board is clamped dead vertical. I spent a month blaming my wrist when it was the vise.

replies.author: mara
replies.content: The mirror trick is brilliant. Joint number eleven had no gaps on the front face. I'm framing it.

topics.author: tomas
topics.title: Which finish for a kitchen table that gets abused daily?
topics.content: Oak table, three kids, one dog, lots of spilled juice. Polyurethane looks plastic to me, but oil seems too delicate. What has held up for you?

replies.author: ozan
replies.content: Hardwax oil. It looks and feels like oil, resists water well, and when a spot wears out you sand that spot and re-oil it. No stripping the whole top.

replies.author: mara
replies.content: Seconding hardwax oil. Two thin coats, buffed, and a third on the top only.

replies.author: june
replies.content: Whatever you choose, test it on an offcut with a glass of juice left overnight. Learned that one the hard way.

topics.author: tomas
topics.title: MIG or flux-core for a beginner on a budget?
topics.content: I want to weld small projects: a log rack, brackets, maybe a trailer ramp one day. Is a gasless flux-core machine good enough to learn on, or should I save for a MIG with gas?

replies.author: ozan
replies.content: Flux-core is a fine way to learn and works outside in the wind, where gas gets blown away. Expect more spatter and a slag layer to chip off. If you can, buy a machine that can do both later.

replies.author: eli
replies.content: Whatever you buy, budget for a good auto-darkening helmet and gloves first. Your eyes are not upgradeable.

topics.author: eli
topics.title: Restoring a 1970s radio: loud hum on every station
topics.content:
Picked up a 1974 table radio at a flea market. It powers up, the dial lights, every station comes through, but there is a loud 100 Hz hum underneath. Volume knob makes no difference to the hum.

Where would you start?

replies.author: ozan
replies.content: Hum that doesn't change with volume, at twice mains frequency, is the classic sign of dried-out filter capacitors in the power supply. Discharge them before touching anything.

replies.author: eli
replies.content: That was it. Replaced the two big electrolytics and it is dead quiet now. The old ones had visibly bulged tops.

replies.author: priya
replies.content: Love this. Please post a photo of the cabinet, those 70s designs are gorgeous.

topics.author: june
topics.title: Crawling glaze on the rim, what am I doing wrong?
topics.content:
My last batch of mugs came out with bare patches where the glaze pulled back into beads, mostly near the rim. Same glaze worked fine last month.

Bisque was the same temperature. The only change: I glazed them a day after bisque instead of the same week.

replies.author: priya
replies.content: Dust or oil on the bisque is the usual suspect. Did you handle the rims a lot? Try wiping with a damp sponge before glazing.

replies.author: ozan
replies.content: Also check application thickness. Crawling loves a thick coat that cracks while drying.

replies.author: june
replies.content: Sponged everything and dipped for two seconds instead of four. No crawling in the new batch. Thank you!

topics.author: priya
topics.title: Saddle stitching tips for a first leather wallet
topics.content: I am making my first bifold wallet from 1.2 mm veg-tan. Stitching chisels arrived today. Anything you wish someone had told you before your first saddle stitch?

replies.author: mara
replies.content: Wax the thread even if it is pre-waxed, and keep the same over-under order for every stitch or the line looks uneven.

replies.author: june
replies.content: Punch through both layers together so the holes line up. Glue first, then punch.

topics.author: ozan
topics.title: Show us your bench (mess included)
topics.content: No tidying allowed. Describe or post your workbench exactly as it is right now. I'll start: three clamps, a cold coffee, half a radio and a drawing of a chair I will never build.

replies.author: mara
replies.content: Spoon blanks in a plastic bag, a hatchet, and the dovetail practice board I refuse to throw away.

replies.author: tomas
replies.content: A welding helmet, one sock (why?) and my kid's lego spaceship which I have been told not to touch.

replies.author: eli
replies.content: Soldering station, magnifier, a pile of resistors I swear I will sort one day.

replies.author: june
replies.content: Clay dust on everything. Literally everything.
